titleOptions: How Nokia Lost Everything in Six Years
Nokia Saw the iPhone Coming. It Was Too Scared to Stop It.
chosenTitle: How Nokia Lost Everything in Six Years
hook: In 2007, one of every two smartphones sold on Earth was a Nokia. Six years later, it sold its entire phone business for about half of what Apple made in a single month. Here's the part nobody tells you: Nokia saw the future coming. It had already built it. It was just too afraid to ship it.

beats.heading: Cold open: the king of phones
beats.narration: Half the world's smartphones, and a brand people trusted more than their banks.

beats.heading: The rise: rubber boots to world domination
beats.narration: From a Finnish paper mill to the company that put a phone in a billion pockets.

beats.heading: The warning: a touchscreen in 2004
beats.narration: Nokia engineers had a touchscreen, internet-ready phone years before the iPhone, and management shelved it.

beats.heading: The fall: fear in the middle
beats.narration: Researchers later found a company where nobody dared tell the boss bad news.

beats.heading: The burning platform
beats.narration: A new CEO, a famous memo, and a bet on Windows Phone that came too late.

beats.heading: The lesson
beats.narration: Companies rarely die from not seeing the future. They die from being afraid to act on it.

scenes.narration: In 2007, one of every two smartphones sold on Earth was a Nokia.
scenes.visual: Black screen, then archive footage of crowded mid-2000s city streets with people holding Nokia phones. Kinetic text: 1 IN 2.

scenes.narration: Six years later, it sold its entire phone business for about half of what Apple made in a single month.
scenes.visual: Motion graphic: Nokia logo shrinking next to an Apple revenue bar for one month of 2013.

scenes.narration: Here's the part nobody tells you. Nokia saw the future coming. It had already built it.
scenes.visual: Slow push-in on a generic early prototype touchscreen device on a desk, dramatic side light.

scenes.narration: It was just too afraid to ship it. This is how the most powerful phone company in history broke.
scenes.visual: A cracked phone screen in slow motion. Title card: BUILT & BROKEN, NOKIA.

scenes.narration: Nokia didn't start with phones. In 1865 it was a paper mill on a Finnish river, named after the town of Nokia.
scenes.visual: Public-domain photos of 19th-century Finnish paper mills and the Nokianvirta river. Map pin on Finland.

scenes.narration: Over the next century it made rubber boots, car tyres and electrical cable. Then in the 1980s, it went all in on a strange new idea: phones you could carry.
scenes.visual: Archive product shots: rubber boots, tyres, cables, then a 1980s brick mobile phone.

scenes.narration: The man who made that bet was Jorma Ollila, a former banker who became CEO in 1992 when Nokia was close to collapse. He sold off almost everything that wasn't telecom.
scenes.visual: Archive-style photo montage of early-1990s Helsinki, a boardroom, and a stack of divisions being crossed out on a chart.

scenes.narration: Finland's timing was perfect. The Nordic countries had pioneered shared mobile networks, and Europe was agreeing on one digital standard, GSM, that let a phone work across borders.
scenes.visual: Animated map of Europe lighting up country by country with GSM network coverage.

scenes.narration: By 1998, Nokia had become the biggest mobile phone maker in the world. It would hold that crown for well over a decade.
scenes.visual: Animated line chart: Nokia market share climbing past Motorola in 1998.

scenes.narration: The phones were indestructible. The batteries lasted a week. The ringtone became the most-heard melody on the planet.
scenes.visual: Stock footage of a sturdy 2000s handset dropped on concrete, then a phone ringing on a cafe table.

scenes.narration: Nokia sold phones for every pocket, from fifty-dollar handsets in India and Nigeria to luxury models in London. In emerging markets, Nokia simply was the mobile phone.
scenes.visual: Stock footage of busy markets in Lagos and Mumbai with phone stalls; world map with sales hot spots.

scenes.narration: At its peak, the company was so big that it was responsible for roughly a quarter of Finland's exports.
scenes.visual: Motion graphic: Finland export bar, with a quarter of it filled in Nokia blue.

scenes.narration: And Nokia didn't just sell basic phones. It practically invented the smartphone. Its Symbian software ran on the majority of smartphones sold in the mid-2000s.
scenes.visual: Motion graphic: pie chart of 2007 smartphone operating systems, Symbian taking about half.

scenes.narration: Back in 1996, its Communicator could already send email, fax and browse a basic web. Nokia was building pocket computers before most people had heard the phrase.
scenes.visual: Illustration of a 1990s clamshell business phone opened like a mini laptop on an airplane tray table.

scenes.narration: In 2007, Nokia's stock market value peaked at well over one hundred billion dollars. It was Europe's most valuable tech company.
scenes.visual: Animated stock chart rising to a 2007 peak, with a gold glow on the high point.

scenes.narration: Then, in January 2007, Steve Jobs walked on stage and pulled out a phone with no keyboard.
scenes.visual: Stock footage of a keynote stage and audience silhouettes (no Apple footage). Text: JANUARY 9, 2007.

scenes.narration: Here's the twist. Nokia's own engineers had shown management a touchscreen, internet-ready phone back in 2004, according to former employees who later spoke to the Wall Street Journal.
scenes.visual: Illustrated mock-up of a 2004-era touchscreen prototype on a meeting table, executives' hands around it.

scenes.narration: Management passed. It looked expensive and risky, and Nokia was already winning. Why bet on something new?
scenes.visual: Kinetic text over a dim boardroom: TOO EXPENSIVE. TOO RISKY. WE'RE WINNING.

scenes.narration: When the iPhone arrived, many Nokia leaders dismissed it. It was too pricey, the battery was weak, and it couldn't even send a picture message.
scenes.visual: Split screen: spec comparison table of 2007 phones animating in, with Nokia ticking more boxes.

scenes.narration: On paper they were right. Nokia's phones had better cameras, better batteries and better networks. But customers weren't buying specs. They were buying how it felt to use.
scenes.visual: Stock footage of hands swiping and pinching on a touchscreen, close-up, warm light.

scenes.narration: And there was a deeper problem. Nokia was a hardware company. It measured success in units shipped, factory costs and how tough a phone was. Software was something you bolted on at the end.
scenes.visual: Factory assembly line footage, conveyor of phone shells; overlay labels: UNITS, COSTS, DURABILITY.

scenes.narration: Apple flipped that. The iPhone was software first, with hardware built around it. Nokia's culture was built for the opposite world.
scenes.visual: Motion graphic: two stacked layers, HARDWARE and SOFTWARE, swapping places.

scenes.narration: So why couldn't a company with billions of dollars and thousands of brilliant engineers respond?
scenes.visual: Slow aerial of a glass corporate campus in winter. Text: WHY?

scenes.narration: Years later, two researchers from INSEAD and Aalto University interviewed 76 Nokia managers and engineers. What they found wasn't stupidity. It was fear.
scenes.visual: Motion graphic: a stack of interview transcripts with the word FEAR highlighted.

scenes.narration: Top executives were known for their temper. Middle managers learned that bad news could cost them their jobs, so they told leaders what they wanted to hear.
scenes.visual: Silhouettes in a corridor, a door closing on a meeting room. Muted colour grade.

scenes.narration: Engineers knew Symbian was ageing and painful to build for. Leadership kept hearing that the next version would be ready soon.
scenes.visual: Animated timeline of promised software release dates sliding later and later.

scenes.narration: Meanwhile, Apple's App Store and Google's free Android were pulling developers away. Phones were becoming computers, and computers live or die on software.
scenes.visual: Motion graphic: app icons flowing from a Nokia phone into two rival app stores.

scenes.narration: Nokia did try to build an answer. It launched Ovi, its own app and music store, and started a new operating system called MeeGo.
scenes.visual: Generic illustrated app store grid on an older phone screen, with a progress bar stuck at sixty percent.

scenes.narration: But different teams fought over which software would win, and projects were reorganised again and again. Inside the company, people called it a war of platforms.
scenes.visual: Animated org chart with boxes rearranging repeatedly and arrows pointing at each other.

scenes.narration: By 2010, Nokia's smartphone share was collapsing, and the board hired a new CEO from Microsoft, Stephen Elop.
scenes.visual: Chart: Symbian market share falling 2008 to 2010. Text card: NEW CEO, 2010.

scenes.narration: In February 2011 he sent staff a memo that leaked to the world. Nokia, he wrote, was standing on a burning platform.
scenes.visual: Typewriter-style animated text of the phrase BURNING PLATFORM over an offshore oil rig at night.

scenes.narration: His answer was to abandon Nokia's own software and bet everything on Microsoft's Windows Phone.
scenes.visual: Motion graphic: Nokia logo jumping from one platform to another as the old one burns.

scenes.narration: The memo was brutally honest, and it also had a side effect. Telling the world your current phones are on fire is not great for selling them. Symbian sales fell off a cliff.
scenes.visual: Chart: Symbian sales dropping sharply in 2011 right after a memo icon appears on the timeline.

scenes.narration: The cruel irony came months later. Nokia released the N9 on MeeGo, a phone critics loved, and then barely sold it, because the company had already committed to Windows.
scenes.visual: Illustrated sleek 2011 smartphone in a glass display with a rope barrier in front of it.

scenes.narration: The Lumia phones that followed were well made and colourful. But Windows Phone had a fraction of the apps people wanted, and shoppers walked past them to buy iPhones and Android phones.
scenes.visual: Stock footage of a phone shop, customers picking up other phones while one bright display table sits untouched.

scenes.narration: It was too late. Developers didn't follow, customers didn't switch, and sales kept falling.
scenes.visual: Empty shop shelf with dust, slow dolly. Falling bar chart overlay.

scenes.narration: In September 2013, Microsoft agreed to buy Nokia's phone business for about 5.4 billion euros, roughly seven billion dollars.
scenes.visual: Animated headline card: DEAL ANNOUNCED, €5.44B, with the date.

scenes.narration: Two years later Microsoft wrote most of that value off. The phones that once ruled the world quietly disappeared from shops.
scenes.visual: Old handsets in a recycling bin, slow motion. Text: WRITTEN OFF.

scenes.narration: From the 2007 peak, Nokia's market value had fallen by roughly ninety percent. Tens of thousands of jobs disappeared, many of them in Finland.
scenes.visual: Stock chart falling from the 2007 peak to 2012, then quiet footage of a snowy, empty Finnish office park.

scenes.narration: But here's what surprises people. Nokia didn't die. It went back to what it knew, networks, and today builds the equipment that carries mobile data around the world.
scenes.visual: Stock footage of 5G cell towers at golden hour, network lines animating between cities.

scenes.narration: The phone giant was gone, though, and the reason is a warning for every successful company.
scenes.visual: Slow fade over a lone vintage Nokia handset on a table.

scenes.narration: Look at the timeline again. A touchscreen prototype in 2004. Smartphone software leadership in 2007. A critically loved phone in 2011. At every step, Nokia had the pieces.
scenes.visual: Animated timeline revisiting each milestone, each one lighting gold then dimming.

scenes.narration: Nokia didn't lose because it couldn't see the future. It had built the future in its own labs.
scenes.visual: Callback: the prototype illustration from scene 12, now behind glass like a museum piece.

scenes.narration: It lost because the people who saw it were too afraid to say so, and the people in charge were too comfortable to listen.
scenes.visual: Kinetic text: TOO AFRAID TO SAY. TOO COMFORTABLE TO LISTEN.

outro: Next on Built & Broken: Kodak invented the digital camera in 1975, then told the inventor to keep quiet. Subscribe so you don't miss how that story ends.
